notes.meaning: God gives a direct message to Joel, the son of Pethuel. Joel claims no special power of his own, acting only as a voice to deliver what the Lord commanded. Mentioning his father helps distinguish him from other men of the same name. Believers are reminded to listen humbly when God speaks through His word.

The prophet calls on the oldest community leaders and all who live in the land to pay close attention. The older men have seen the most life, yet even they have never witnessed a calamity so severe. The disaster is so remarkable that parents must tell their children, passing the story down through four generations. Remembering God's past judgments helps teach each new generation to revere Him.

Wave after wave of locusts sweeps across the land, leaving nothing behind. Each swarm eats whatever green growth the previous swarm spared, until every field is stripped clean. God can use the smallest, weakest insects to humble a proud and rebellious nation.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some older Catholic commentators saw the four types of locusts as symbols of four successive foreign invasions, especially the repeated attacks of the Babylonians.

notes.meaning: Heavy drinkers are told to shake off their drunken stupor and weep out loud. The swarms have destroyed the grape harvest, cutting off their supply of sweet wine before it can reach their lips. When people live only for sensory pleasure, God may take away the very things they abuse.

The locusts advance like a massive, organized army invading the Lord's land. They tear into vegetation with teeth as destructive as lions' fangs, chewing away leaves and bark until the tree limbs turn bare and white. God's people are forced to see how quickly their most treasured fruit trees can be ruined when His protection is withdrawn.

The entire land is called to mourn with deep and bitter tears. The people should grieve like a young bride whose bridegroom dies right before or soon after their wedding. Sackcloth was a scratchy, dark cloth worn to show great personal sadness. Their sorrow over sin and its consequences must be real and profound, not just an empty show.

Daily offerings of grain and wine have stopped at the temple because the fields are completely empty. The priests mourn deeply because they can no longer perform the sacrifices commanded by God. The loss of these gifts marks a painful interruption in the outward signs of fellowship with the Lord.

The farmland lies broken and is pictured as weeping over the loss of its crops. Grain for bread, grapes for wine, and olives for oil have all failed at once. Because the people took God's basic blessings for granted, they now feel the sting of absolute shortage.

Farmers and vineyard keepers stand dismayed and weeping because all their hard work has produced nothing. The staple grains of wheat and barley are gone, and even hardy fruit trees like pomegranates, date palms, and apples have withered away. When the harvest perishes, the normal singing and joyful celebration of the harvest season dry up entirely.

The priests are told to put on rough sackcloth and spend the whole night weeping before the altar. As spiritual leaders, they must set the example for the rest of the nation in seeking God's mercy. Because the daily worship supplies are gone, they must plead with God to restore His favor to His house.

The priests must announce a holy fast, a time when people go without food to focus entirely on prayer. All the elders and ordinary citizens are summoned to the temple in Jerusalem to seek God together. In times of widespread crisis, God's people must unite in humble confession and cry out for His help.

The prophet cries out in dread because this devastation is a warning sign that the Day of the Lord is close at hand. That day is a decisive time when God steps in to judge unrepentant people with irresistible power. The present disaster comes directly from the Almighty, showing that no human effort can resist His righteous judgment.

differ.view: The day of the Lord refers to God coming in historical judgment against His unfaithful covenant people, warning that outward religious status cannot protect them from His wrath.
This verse points forward to the end-times Great Tribulation, when God will pour out global judgments just before Jesus Christ returns to reign on earth.

notes.meaning: The prophet bids the people to face the hard facts right in front of them. Their food has vanished before their eyes, and the happy songs of the sacred festivals have ended. When worship at God's house is silenced, true joy disappears from a nation.

A terrible drought follows the locust attack, causing the seeds to shrivel and rot under the dry dirt. Granaries and storage barns sit in ruins because there is no grain to store inside them. Cattle wander about in distress and sheep suffer terribly because there is no green pasture left to graze.

Joel turns directly to God in personal prayer, even if others remain stubborn and unmoved. Blistering heat has scorched the open grazing fields like a blaze, and streams have run completely dry. Even wild animals pant toward heaven for moisture, and their instinctive cries shame people who refuse to pray.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The fire and flames are understood as poetic descriptions of extreme heat and drought that left the countryside looking as if it had been consumed by a wildfire.
